newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S.LEONE COUP LEADERS TO NEGOTIATE WITH NIGERIANS.
newsitem.headline: S.LEONE COUP LEADERS TO NEGOTIATE WITH NIGERIANS.

text.p: Sierra Leone's coup leaders, under threat of a military strike to reverse their week-old takeover, will hold talks later on Sunday with Nigerian officials to seek a negotiated settlement.
One official said the talks would involve a much larger group than the delegation that made a first contact with the Nigerians on Saturday.
Sierra Leonean politicians involved in the negotiations said coup leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah was likely to attend. "Koromah wants to do a deal," said one source.

Helicopters from a U.S. Navy ship off Freetown completed the evacuation of remaining Americans and Europeans who took refuge in two beachside hotels from the widespread looting and violence which followed last Sunday's coup.
"All those that wanted to go were evacuated," Commodore Greg Ertel said from the U.S.S. Kearsarge.

The Sierra Leonean sources spoke of growing disagreement between the coup leaders and rebels of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) who have joined forces with the army but firmly oppose any negotiated settlement.
One source said two people had been killed in gunfights between RUF rebels and coup soldiers inside the military headquarters where Koromah and his colleagues have been holed up since seizing power.
RUF rebels, recognisable from their matted hair, black gloves and red headbands, were increasingly visible around the capital, proudly manning road checkpoints.

They have taken no part in contacts with the Nigerians so far as it was not clear whether they would join Sunday's talks, due to start at the residence of Nigerian ambassador Chidi Abubakar at noon (1200 GMT).

The last Westerners seeking evacuation were airlifted from the grounds of the Mammy Yoko Hotel, where anxious Nigerian, Ghanaian and Gambian residents milled around with their consular officers looking for ways to get them out.
A privately chartered boat docked nearby was expected to carry Lebanese nationals to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea, later on Sunday.

One group of European arrived in Italy on Sunday from Conakry. "Some of the rebels shot at the door of my room to try and get in," Briton Joe Dogherty from Bath told Italian reporters at Rome's main Fiumicino airport.
"Others had their houses looted. We had problems getting food, all the shops were closed or burned. There were armed men in the streets and we all sought refuge where we could."

The coup leaders sent a delegation to the Nigerian ambassador on Saturday as military sources reported a contingent of Guinean troops entered Sierra Leone to join the Nigerian-led regional force gearing up to reverse the coup.

"Basically they wanted assurances of safe conduct outside the country and possible asylum," said a source close to the talks. The army delegation included the number two in the new Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Captain Paul Thomas.
"The ambassador told them Nigeria would consider their request but could not speak for other countries on the issue of asylum," the source said.
Diplomats said representatives of the coup leaders also held talks with British envoys and U.N. officials.

The United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and the West African alliance ECOWAS have condemned the coup and called for restoration of power to President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who fled to Guinea.
ECOMOG, whose main mandate is keeping peace in Liberia, now has about 3,000 men in Sierra Leone, backed by Nigerian ships as well as helicopters based in Liberia.
Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United Nations James Jonah said he suspected Liberians had masterminded the coup.

"It is suspected that they are Liberian because when they speak on radio they have a Liberian accent," Jonah told Zimbabwe state media on Saturday when he arrived to represent Kabbah at an Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit opening on Monday.
Jonah said he would lobby at the summit for concrete steps to reverse the coup, Sierra Leone's third in five years.
